title: Feasibility — research-grounded study-swarm verdict (seeded from wf_965f110f-e24)
domain_scope: MoE + dense placement methodology, the Windows/WSL CUDA-UVM premise, and prediction/receipt honesty for the gpu-container planner
verifier_note: 3-lens, reasoning-stripped: WebFetch retrieval oracle (existence + attribution) + mistral-small:24b (Mistral) + granite4.1:30b (IBM Granite) for groundedness. This is the FAMILY-DIFFERENT verification that the sibling KBs (tensor-engine, model) defer to their P1 backlog. 35 unique sources, 0 fabricated. Dropped 1 misattribution (Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing arXiv:2408.15664 — real paper, but the inference-skew claim is not in it) and 1 source for unsupported numbers (localllm.in).
notes: Seeded from the gpu-container feasibility study-swarm. Full synthesis lives at gpu-container/docs/feasibility.md. Verdict: PASS with three required calibrations.

research.domain: Tiered MoE expert offload (hot-VRAM / warm-RAM / cold-NVMe) + skew, prefetch, eviction on one consumer GPU
research.notes: The flagship lane. The warm tier is production-proven and already shipping; the cold-NVMe tier is conditional on accurate prefetch + sparsity. Two non-negotiable design constraints fell out: calibration must be adaptive (skew is request-level), and expert eviction must be staleness-aware (not LRU).

findings.name: Warm-tier MoE offload is production-proven
findings.claim: Hot-VRAM + warm-RAM expert placement (or CPU expert compute) clears the >1 tok/s floor on a single consumer GPU today.
findings.detail: Fiddler runs uncompressed Mixtral-8x7B (90GB+) at >3 tok/s on one 24GB GPU by computing cold experts on CPU instead of moving weights over PCIe; KTransformers runs DeepSeek-V3 671B at ~8.7-10 tok/s decode on a 4090D + 382GB RAM; llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe field-reports ~12-14 tok/s on huge MoEs; Mixtral-offloading hits 2-3 tok/s on consumer/Colab and is PCIe host-to-device bound.
findings.design_implication: The hot/warm tier is a safe throughput claim; llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe is the first integration target.

findings.name: Cold-NVMe expert streaming is the danger zone
findings.claim: Streaming cold experts from NVMe during decode is feasible only with accurate prefetch + sparsity; otherwise it thrashes.
findings.detail: SSD expert offload raises per-token-generation energy ~12x vs an HBM baseline, and prefetching hides latency but NOT the energy/bandwidth penalty. PowerInfer-2 reaches 9.96 tok/s with 50% of FFN on flash by overlapping I/O with compute — but only with a custom SPARSIFIED model with predictable activation.
findings.design_implication: Gate the cold-NVMe tier: admit only if predicted prefetch hit-rate keeps decode above the floor; default it off for experts otherwise.
findings.metric: ~12x per-token energy vs HBM; 9.96 tok/s at 50% FFN on flash (sparsified)

findings.name: Expert skew is real but request-level (calibration must be adaptive)
findings.claim: MoE activation is skewed within a request (<5% of experts) but aggregates toward uniform across diverse prompts.
findings.detail: MoE-Infinity measures <5% of experts repeatedly activated per request, but is explicit that the skew is request-level and flattens to uniform when aggregated across many diverse prompts. A one-time global frequency histogram therefore mis-tiers out-of-distribution workloads and thrashes the warm tier.
findings.design_implication: Calibration #1: calibrate on workload-representative traces and refine online from the receipt's measured routing — NOT a single generic-corpus snapshot.
findings.metric: <5% experts active per request; 3.1-16.7x per-token latency improvement

sources.title: MoE-Infinity: Efficient MoE Inference on Personal Machines with Sparsity-Aware Expert Cache
sources.claim: <5% experts active per request; activation-traced cache gives 3.1-16.7x per-token latency improvement; skew is request-level and aggregates to uniform.

findings.name: Router lookahead hides the RAM->VRAM transfer
findings.claim: A router can predict next-layer experts during the current layer, overlapping the warm-tier transfer with compute.
findings.detail: Pre-gated MoE selects the next layer's experts during the current layer, landing within 19% of GPU-only latency at 4.2x memory reduction with quality preserved; Fate reaches ~99% expert hit-rate (4.1x decode speedup); MoE-Beyond lifts cache hit from 17% to 72% with only 10% of experts resident.
findings.design_implication: A small VRAM hot tier + router-lookahead prefetch is sufficient — the warm tier need not be large.
findings.metric: within 19% of GPU-only (Pre-gated); ~99% hit (Fate); 17%->72% hit at 10% resident (MoE-Beyond)

sources.title: Pre-gated MoE: Algorithm-System Co-Design for Fast & Scalable MoE Inference
sources.claim: Pre-gate selects next-layer experts in the current layer; within 19% of GPU-only latency, 4.2x memory cut, quality preserved.

sources.title: Fate: Fast Edge Inference of MoE Models via Cross-Layer Gate
sources.claim: Adjacent-layer gate prefetch + shallow cache -> ~99% hit rate, up to 4.1x decode speedup vs load-on-demand.

sources.title: MoE-Beyond: Learning-Based Expert Activation Prediction on Edge Devices
sources.claim: Sequence-prediction prefetch ~97.5% accuracy; GPU cache hit 17%->72% at 10% experts resident.

findings.name: Expert eviction must be staleness-aware, not LRU
findings.claim: MoE expert access is deterministic-sequential, not recency-based, so LRU/LFU evicts the wrong experts.
findings.detail: SpecMD finds expert access is deterministic-sequential rather than temporal-locality-based; a Least-Stale eviction policy cuts collision misses up to 85x vs LRU and reaches >88% hit at only 5% (0.6GB) VRAM cache.
findings.design_implication: Calibration #1: use a staleness/sequence-aware eviction policy for experts. (LRU/ARC remains correct for KV-cache spill — it is wrong for experts.)
findings.metric: 85x fewer collision misses vs LRU; >88% hit at 5% VRAM

sources.title: SpecMD: A Comprehensive Study on Speculative Expert Prefetching
sources.claim: Expert access is deterministic-sequential (not recency); Least-Stale eviction cuts misses up to 85x vs LRU, >88% hit at 5% VRAM.

research.domain: The Windows/WSL CUDA Unified-Memory premise — the product's load-bearing positioning
research.notes: The moat. NVIDIA's own docs confirm both halves: UVM oversubscription is unavailable on Windows/WSL2, and even where it exists (Linux) it is catastrophically slow for bandwidth-bound decode. This is the strongest-verified part of the study (oracle + both families concurred on the NVIDIA-docs facts).

findings.name: No CUDA UVM oversubscription on Windows/WSL2
findings.claim: Full managed-memory oversubscription is unavailable on Windows native and WSL2 by driver design (WDDM).
findings.detail: NVIDIA's CUDA-on-WSL guide states verbatim that Full Managed Memory is unavailable on Windows native and WSL2 'for the foreseeable future' and warns of reduced performance / high host-memory use. The CUDA C++ Programming Guide formalizes the split: Linux allows managed-memory oversubscription; Windows/WSL/Tegra do not (cudaDevAttrConcurrentManagedAccess == 0), and such devices cannot allocate more managed memory than physical VRAM (oversubscription needs CC 6.0+ page faulting).
findings.design_implication: Explicit, declared placement is the ONLY honest route on the target platform — this is NOT 'Docker VRAM overflow'. The whole product positioning rests here, and it is primary-sourced.

sources.title: CUDA on WSL User Guide (NVIDIA)
sources.claim: Full Managed Memory unavailable on Windows native and WSL2 'for the foreseeable future'; managed-memory apps see reduced perf + high host-mem use.

sources.title: CUDA C++ Programming Guide — Unified/System Memory + Oversubscription
sources.claim: Linux = full UM, oversubscription allowed; Windows/WSL/Tegra = limited, oversubscription NOT allowed; needs CC 6.0+ page faulting.

findings.name: Even on Linux, UVM oversubscription is wrong for decode
findings.claim: On-demand page-migrated UVM collapses effective bandwidth by orders of magnitude — fatal for bandwidth-bound decode.
findings.detail: NVIDIA's own oversubscription blog reports performance can vary up to 100x; on-demand migration falls from ~8-10 GB/s to ~1 GB/s at 2x oversubscription, and random access drops to a few hundred KB/s — vs the hundreds of GB/s decode needs. Chien et al. measured basic UM 9-14x slower than explicit even before oversubscription; GPUVM (2024) confirms stock demand-paging is a known bottleneck being re-engineered. Decode is bandwidth-bound (the Memory Wall).
findings.design_implication: Explicit declared placement beats blind demand-paging decisively even where UVM exists — confirms the architecture, not just the platform constraint.
findings.metric: up to 100x variation; ~8-10 -> ~1 GB/s at 2x oversub; random to hundreds of KB/s

sources.claim: Oversubscription perf varies up to 100x; on-demand migration ~8-10 -> ~1 GB/s at 2x; random warp access to a few hundred KB/s.

research.domain: Can memory + decode throughput be predicted accurately enough pre-launch for an honest refusal and a +/-10% receipt?
research.notes: Memory is exact; throughput splits sharply by offload regime. Scope the tight receipt to in-VRAM/light-offload.

findings.name: Memory is exact; throughput prediction splits by offload regime
findings.claim: KV/weight memory is closed-form; throughput is predictable to ~10% in-VRAM but only ~1.5-2x under heavy NVMe offload.
findings.detail: KV-cache is closed-form/linear in context (NVIDIA). In-VRAM, Vidur predicts P95 latency within 3.33%. Under heavy offload, static analytical prediction is documented insufficient: roofline over-predicts and needs measured calibration (Imai 2024); FlexGen's own LP 'can run out of memory' and is 'beaten by tuning manually'; LLM-Pilot (a learned predictor) meets its target only 80% of the time; NVMe random QD1-4 is far below sequential, so a sequential assumption over-predicts decode by multiples.
findings.design_implication: Calibration #2: guarantee the +/-10% receipt only for in-VRAM/light-offload; label heavy-NVMe plans 'estimated, receipt-confirmed'; make refusal conservative; the receipt->recalibration loop is load-bearing.
findings.metric: 3.33% P95 in-VRAM (Vidur); 80% target-hit (LLM-Pilot); roofline insufficient w/o calibration

sources.claim: Predicts P95 latency within 3.33% (static) for in-GPU serving; assumes model fits in VRAM.

research.domain: Single-stream throughput envelope for dense models too big for VRAM, and the latency-vs-throughput tension
research.notes: Dense offload tiers off a cliff; the seminal wins are throughput-at-large-batch, not single-stream latency.

findings.name: Dense offload tiers off a cliff; NVMe spill is sub-1 tok/s
findings.claim: Single-stream dense decode falls roughly linearly with RAM offload and collapses below 1 tok/s once weights stream from NVMe.
findings.detail: ~150 tok/s fully in VRAM (8B int4) -> ~60-70% at 20/32 layers on GPU -> ~3-6 tok/s for 70B on DDR5 partial offload -> sub-1 tok/s once dense weights stream from NVMe (AirLLM: 0.7 tok/s down to ~1 token/hour). The seminal offload wins are throughput-at-large-batch, explicitly 'not suitable for latency sensitive' (FlexGen 1 tok/s on OPT-175B at batch 144; ZeRO-Inference OPT-30B 43 tok/s CPU vs 30 tok/s NVMe, aggregate).
findings.design_implication: Calibration #3: RAM-offload partial is the serviceable dense envelope; reserve NVMe for cold MoE experts, NOT dense weights (dense has no sparsity to exploit).
findings.metric: 150 tok/s VRAM -> 3-6 tok/s 70B RAM-offload -> sub-1 tok/s NVMe

research.domain: The >1 tok/s refusal floor and the measured-receipt -> recalibration loop
research.notes: The floor is correctly calibrated and will fire often for dense+NVMe — by design, not as a failure.

findings.name: The >1 tok/s floor is correct and will refuse dense+NVMe often
findings.claim: A >1 tok/s decode floor is well-justified; for dense models spilling to NVMe it will (correctly) refuse frequently.
findings.detail: Because sub-1 tok/s single-stream is the documented norm once dense weights hit NVMe, the refusal floor fires correctly there. The product must frame dense+NVMe refusal as honesty, not failure, and surface it with a contrastive frame ('you expected model X to run; it won't clear 1 tok/s because... — options: smaller quant / more RAM / different model').
findings.design_implication: Position NVMe as the cold-MoE-expert lane, not a dense-weight-streaming lane; the measured receipt is the external verifier of the planner's own prediction (different mechanism, never self-grading).

sources.title: DeepSpeed-Inference: Enabling Efficient Inference at Unprecedented Scale
sources.claim: The offload design space (ZeRO-Inference family) is engineered for aggregate throughput at large batch, not single-stream latency.

verdicts.name: The >1 tok/s floor is correct and will refuse dense+NVMe often
verdicts.note: DeepSpeed-Inference throughput-orientation confirmed; floor justification follows from the dense-offload + memory-wall findings.
